parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A woman phones a car club to join a car-sharing scheme.
script: Good morning, GreenWheel Car Club, Oliver speaking. How can I help you?

Oh, hello. I'm thinking of joining the club, and I wondered whether I could sign up over the phone. A colleague of mine sold her car last year and says she's never looked back, so I thought I'd give it a try.
Certainly, I can take all your details now, and it only takes about ten minutes. Could I have your full name to start with?
Is that Lindquist, with a Q and a U?
No, it's a bit unusual, I'm afraid. It's L-I-N-D-Q-V-I-S-T. My grandfather was Swedish.
Lindqvist. Got it, thanks. And your address?
Flat 4, 18 Quarry Road, in Horsham. The postcode is RH12 3PW.
RH12 3PW. Lovely. Now, we have three membership plans, so it helps to know how often you expect to use a car.
Not very often, to be honest. Probably a couple of times a month, for a big shop at the retail park, and the odd weekend away.

Then I'd suggest the Basic plan. The Standard plan is 12 pounds a month and includes two hours of free driving, but that's really for people who are out in the car every week. The Basic plan is only 9 pounds 50 a month, and you simply pay for the hours you use.
Oh, that sounds much better for me. I'll take the Basic one, then.
Great. Now, where would you collect the cars from? We have bays at the station and at the market square, but the closest one to Quarry Road is in the car park behind the library on Mill Lane.
Oh, that's only five minutes on foot. I thought the nearest one was at the leisure centre.
It was, but that site closed in March, so you'll need the library one now. Next, how long have you held your driving licence? We ask for at least 2 years.
Oh, much longer than that. I passed my test nearly 11 years ago.
That's absolutely fine, then. Is there a particular type of car you'd like? We have hatchbacks and estates, and two small vans.
I did think about a van, because I'm planning to move a bookcase next month, but I can hire one separately for that. So a hatchback, please. That's what I'm used to driving.
A hatchback it is. Now, the money side. There's a refundable deposit of 50 pounds, which we take with your first payment. It used to be 75, but we reduced it at the beginning of the year.
That's good to know. And what happens if I have an accident?
Insurance is included in the membership, but there's an excess of 250 pounds. Some members pay 15 pounds extra a year to bring that down to 100, but most don't bother.
I'll stay with the standard excess, I think.
Fine. And on the Basic plan the driving rate is 4 pounds 20 an hour. That includes the fuel, and you only start paying for distance after the first 60 miles of a booking.
That seems reasonable. How do I actually book a car?
Everything is done through our app. You choose the bay, the day and the time, and you unlock the car with your membership card. We'll post the card to you within five working days.
Lovely. Is there anything else I need to do before then?

Just one thing. Every new member comes to a short induction at the Mill Lane bay. The next one is on Saturday morning at 10. We check your licence online, so you don't need to bring that, but please bring your passport so we can confirm your identity.
My passport. Right. I'll be there on Saturday. Thank you very much for your help, Oliver.
You're very welcome, Nadia. Welcome to the club.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A radio presenter reports on a community bakery run by the residents of a village.
script: Hello and welcome to Community Matters. This week I'm in the village of Larkfield, where for the last four years the residents have been running their own bakery. I spent a morning there, and I'd like to tell you how it works, because I think it's a story that a lot of towns could learn from.

Let me start at the beginning. Larkfield had a bakery for more than a hundred years. When the owner retired, nobody wanted to take it on, and it closed. People had always assumed the village shop would be the next to go, and in fact it did survive, so it wasn't a lack of shopping that worried them. What they missed was fresh bread, and the place where neighbours bumped into each other at eight in the morning. So a small group of residents called a public meeting, and over a hundred people turned up.

The next question was money. They did apply for a lottery grant, but that was only enough to pay for the two big ovens. The building itself, an old bank on the high street, was bought differently. The group sold shares to local people for 50 pounds each, and within three months they'd raised enough. Today there are more than 400 shareholders, and every one of them has a single vote, however many shares they hold. There was a loan offered by the council as well, but the group turned it down, because they wanted to stay independent.

So who actually makes the bread? There are two professional bakers, Giulia and Sam, who work through the night, and they're the only paid staff apart from a part-time manager. Everyone else is a volunteer. Around sixty residents work in the shop, serve in the café, or help with the weekend baking, and they sign up for shifts on a rota. When I visited, a retired teacher was weighing dough, and a teenager was cleaning the trays.

One thing that struck me was how little goes to waste. At first, loaves that hadn't sold by closing time were sold at half price on the following morning. That stopped, because customers began waiting for the cheaper bread. These days, anything left over is turned into croutons and bread puddings, and they're served in the café. Nothing is thrown away, and the café is now the most profitable part of the business.

The bakery is also much more than a shop. The week is busy, so let me take you through it. On Mondays, the bakers deliver fresh loaves to the three care homes in the area, and a volunteer driver takes them round in the bakery's electric van. Tuesday afternoons are for children. Local primary school pupils come in to shape and bake their own rolls. Wednesday is the day for the Baking Club, which is mostly for residents over seventy. Some of them have never baked before, and it's become a kind of weekly social event, with a lot of tea. On Thursday evenings there's live music in the café, with local bands playing while people eat pizza made from the bakery's own dough. There's a recipe swap as well, but that's on the first Friday of each month, so I won't dwell on it. On Fridays, the shop sells out by lunchtime. And on Saturdays, the bakers pack up a stall for the farmers' market in the next town, which has brought in a lot of new customers.

What about the future? The committee did consider opening a second shop in the neighbouring village, but they decided the idea was too risky for now. They've also talked about delivering bread to people's homes. Instead, the project they're most excited about is a scheme for teenagers. Starting in the autumn, young people aged fifteen to eighteen will be able to learn to bake in the evenings and earn a recognised qualification. The manager told me she hopes at least a few of them will end up working there.

Before I finish, I asked the manager what advice she would give to other communities. She said it comes down to being patient. It took two years from that first meeting to the day the doors opened, and there were moments when people almost gave up. But, she added, the first morning, when the queue stretched round the corner, made it all worthwhile. That's all for this week. Next time on Community Matters, we visit a town that has turned its old railway station into a library.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two engineering students and their tutor discuss the testing of a model bridge.
script: Right, Marcus, shall we go through the results from the bridge test before Dr Hollis arrives? I've got the notes from last Thursday.
Yes, please. Honestly, I'm still a bit disappointed. After all that work, the model collapsed with only four kilograms on it.
I know, but it was a useful failure. Do you remember why we chose the triangular truss in the first place? You wanted the arched design, because it looked more impressive.
Well, I liked the arch, I admit, but I accept the truss was the right decision. You showed that it spreads the load through all those little triangles, so it can carry a lot with very little wood.

Exactly. And a lighter bridge scores better in the final comparison, so the saving mattered. The tutor's requirement was just that it had to span sixty centimetres, so there was nothing to stop us choosing the arch.
So the design wasn't the problem. Looking at the video, the wood itself didn't snap anywhere. What happened was the joints at the centre came apart, one after another. The glue just let go.

Yes, I noticed that too. I thought at first that the beams were too thin, but the beams stayed whole, so it's the glue joints. If we make the beams thicker, we only add weight and the same joints would still fail.
Agreed. So what if we cut small triangles of card and glue them over each joint? Gusset plates, they're called, I think. They give the glue a much bigger area to hold on to.
That's a good idea. It's cheap, and it won't add much weight. What about trying a different glue? The tube we used says it needs a full day to cure, and we only left it for six hours.

True. Let's do both, then. Wait for a full day, and add the plates. Now, the other thing I wanted to raise is the way we loaded it. We just kept adding bags of sand, and the last bag was dropped on rather than placed. That sudden jolt could have caused the failure, and it makes the numbers unreliable.
Mm. I'd worried about the weight of the sand as well, but I think the real problem was the sudden jolt, so we need to add the load slowly in steps.
Yes, in small steps, and we should wait ten seconds between each one.
Okay. Now, the deck. We used thick card for the road surface, and it's heavier than we need. If we replace it with thin balsa strips, we could save about thirty grams.
Fine by me. And the end supports? They didn't move at all, so I'd leave them exactly as they are.

Agreed. Don't fix what isn't broken. The weights are a different matter. The sand bags were never accurate, so I think we should ask Mr Patel in the workshop. He's got a set of calibrated steel weights, and he might let us borrow them.
Good thinking. I'll go and see him this afternoon. Oh, here's Dr Hollis now.
Hello, both. Sorry I'm late. I've just had a look at your draft report. Shall we talk about the results first?
Yes. We've decided to repeat the test with some changes, but we wanted to make sure we present the first failure properly.

Good. Now, my main advice is about the stress calculations. At the moment you give the numbers from your predictions and then the numbers from the test in different sections. I'd like you to compare them side by side. Predicted against measured. That's what examiners look for.
So we'd need to go back through our calculations and redo some of them, because we used the wrong beam length in the second table.
Yes, please do. It's better to correct it now than lose marks. And please don't make the introduction too long. A page is plenty.
What about the photographs of the failed bridge? We took about twenty of them, and they're really good.
They are, but you don't want twenty photographs in the main text. Choose the best two for the results section and move the rest to an appendix. That keeps the report tidy.
That makes sense. And the deadline is still the end of next week?
It is. If you finish the second test by Tuesday, you'll have plenty of time to write it up.
We'll aim for that. Thank you, Dr Hollis.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecturer talks about urban farming.
script: Good afternoon, everyone. Today I'd like to talk about urban farming, which is a subject that has moved in the last decade from the edge of environmental discussion to the centre of planning debates in many cities.

Let me begin with a definition. Urban farming simply means growing food, and sometimes raising animals, inside cities or on their edges. It's an old idea. People have always grown vegetables in gardens and on allotments. What is new is the scale, and the technology.

So where does it actually happen? Some people imagine fields in the middle of a city, but space is expensive, so most urban farms use areas that would otherwise be wasted. Disused car parks and wasteland are used, and so are balconies, but by far the commonest location is the rooftops of buildings. A flat roof receives full sunlight, it's out of the way, and a building owner may be glad of the insulation that a layer of soil provides.

A second type is the vertical farm. In these, crops are grown in stacked trays inside a building, often a converted warehouse, with no soil at all. The roots sit in a nutrient solution, a method called hydroponics, and the light comes from LEDs, which are tuned to give the plants only the colours they need. A vertical farm can produce many times more per square metre than an ordinary field.

Now, what are the benefits? The one that is quoted most often is a reduction in transport. Most of the food that supplies a large city travels hundreds of kilometres, so there are emissions at every stage. When lettuces grow a few streets away, the distance they travel is tiny, which cuts what we call food miles. It also means that produce reaches the shop a few hours after picking, so it's fresher.

Let me give you an example. In the city of Kessock, a company took over the top floor of a multistorey car park, put in raised beds, and started growing salad crops. Lettuce was the original plan, and it grew well, but the market for it was crowded and prices were low. So the company changed to herbs, such as basil and coriander, which it now sells to restaurants in the city centre at a much better price.

But it would be wrong to suggest that urban farming has no problems. The first is cost. People assume that the biggest expense is the land, but in an indoor vertical farm the biggest single cost is electricity, because the lights run for most of every day.

The second problem concerns the soil. If you're growing food on a former industrial site, the ground may contain heavy metals left by earlier factories, and plants can take those up. Careful testing is essential, and often the safest solution is to grow in raised beds with imported soil. Rooftop farms avoid this problem, but they have another, which is weight, because wet soil is extremely heavy and many old roofs can't bear it.

Water is a related issue. Growing food needs a lot of it, and in a city that means paying for the public supply. The more successful farms collect rainwater from their own roofs and store it in tanks, and some recycle the water from their hydroponic systems, which cuts consumption by up to ninety per cent.

What about the social side? Studies of community gardens suggest that people who take part feel better, and the greatest effect seems to be on mental health. Taking part reduces stress and loneliness, particularly among older people living alone. Many urban farms also run programmes for schools, and children who help to grow vegetables are more willing to try eating them.

So what is stopping urban farming from expanding? One obstacle is the law. In many cities, rules designed a century ago separate land used for housing and land used for agriculture, and these zoning laws make it hard to get permission to grow food in the centre. Several city councils are now reviewing them.

Finally, a word about how important all this might be. You may read that urban farms could feed a city. A few years ago, some experts thought that up to twenty per cent of a city's vegetables might one day come from within its boundaries. More recent calculations are more cautious, and most researchers now believe that the figure is closer to ten per cent. That is still significant, and it comes with the other benefits I've mentioned. So I'd say that urban farming will not replace traditional agriculture, but it can make cities more resilient. Thank you.

passages.title: The long road to the alphabet
paras: A  Most of us learn to read and write with an alphabet so early in life that we rarely think of it as an invention. Yet for most of human history, writing did not work this way. The earliest scripts, which appeared in Mesopotamia and Egypt more than five thousand years ago, used hundreds of different signs, and mastering them took years of training. Scribes were a small and privileged group, and literacy was a tool of kings, priests and tax collectors rather than of ordinary people. The alphabet, in which a small set of signs stands for individual sounds, changed all this. It made writing something that could be learned in a few weeks.

B  The key idea seems to have emerged not in a great capital but among foreign workers. In the early part of the second millennium BCE, groups of Semitic-speaking labourers worked in the turquoise mines of the Sinai peninsula. They were supervised by Egyptian officials, and some of them evidently learned to read a little Egyptian. They borrowed a handful of hieroglyphs, but they used them in a new way. Instead of letting a picture of a house stand for the idea of a house, they let it stand for the first sound of their own word for house, which was something like bayt. A drawing of an ox's head, called alp in their language, came to represent the sound a. This principle, known as acrophony, was the real breakthrough. It meant that a few dozen pictures could be enough to write anything that could be said, and the script that resulted is now called Proto-Sinaitic.

C  The inscriptions these workers left behind are short and rough. Many were scratched on rock walls or on small statues, and for years nobody could read them. They were deciphered only in the early twentieth century, when a scholar noticed that one group of signs appeared again and again and seemed to match the name of a local goddess. Once that sequence had been read, the values of other signs followed, and it became clear that the writing recorded a Semitic language, not Egyptian.

D  Over the following centuries the new system spread northwards to the Levant, where the coastal city-states we now call Phoenician refined it. The Phoenician script had just twenty-two signs, all of them consonants. There were no letters for vowels, and readers supplied them from context, rather as an English reader can make sense of a word such as bldg. This was no great handicap for a Semitic language, and the script's economy suited merchants, who needed a quick way to write accounts, contracts and labels for cargo. Because Phoenician traders sailed all over the Mediterranean, their script travelled with them, and it was copied, adapted and renamed wherever they landed. Texts were written from right to left, a habit that has survived in the scripts of Hebrew and Arabic.

E  The Greeks adopted the Phoenician script around the eighth century BCE, but it was a poor fit for their language, in which vowels carry much of the meaning. The Greeks solved the problem with an ingenious step. Several Phoenician signs stood for consonant sounds that Greek did not have, and they were reassigned to vowels. The sign called aleph, for example, became alpha and now represented the sound a. The result was the first true alphabet in the modern sense, with a separate letter for every consonant and vowel. At first the direction of writing varied. Some early Greek inscriptions change direction on every line, a style called boustrophedon, which means as the ox ploughs, before left to right became the standard.

F  The Etruscans of northern Italy took the Greek alphabet and adapted it for their own use, and the Romans in turn learned it from the Etruscans. The Romans shaped the letters into the elegant capitals that can still be seen on monuments and public buildings, and as their empire grew, the Latin alphabet went with it. Meanwhile, the Greek alphabet had a second line of descent. In the ninth century CE, missionaries devised a new script for the Slavic languages, based largely on Greek letters. It became known as Cyrillic, and it is still used by hundreds of millions of people today.

G  Why did the alphabet succeed so completely? One answer is that it is simply easier to learn, since fewer than thirty signs are enough for most languages. Yet this explanation is too neat. The Korean script Hangul, designed by scholars at the court of a fifteenth-century king, is arguably the most logical system ever created, but it remained largely confined to Korea. Chinese characters, which are far harder to learn, are still used by more than a billion people. The spread of a script, it seems, depends less on its design than on the power and trade of the people who use it. The Phoenicians were successful merchants, the Greeks and Romans built empires, and missionaries carried Cyrillic and Latin letters wherever they went.

H  The word alphabet is simply the names of the first two Greek letters, alpha and beta, joined together. It is a humbling thought that we do not know the name of a single person who took part in this long process. The first alphabet was invented by workers on the margins of a great civilisation, and every stage after that was a series of small improvements made by people who were trying to solve a practical problem. The story is a reminder that important ideas often come not from the centre of power, but from those who have the most to gain from a simpler way of doing things.

passages.title: Eight arms, one clever mind
paras: A  Keepers at the Pelham Bay Marine Centre had a puzzle. Every few mornings, a fish was missing from one of the tanks, and there was no sign of a thief. Eventually the staff installed a camera, and the footage was astonishing. In the small hours, an octopus called Odile slid out of her own tank through a gap beside a drainage pipe, crossed the floor, climbed into the neighbouring tank, ate a fish and then returned home before the first keeper arrived. The story has been told so often that it has become something of a legend among aquarium staff, but similar escapes have been reported all over the world, and they have made many people ask a serious question: just how intelligent are these animals?

B  On the face of it, the octopus is an unlikely candidate for intelligence. It is a mollusc, a relative of snails and clams, and its ancestors lived inside heavy shells. Yet an octopus has around 500 million neurons, a figure comparable to that of a dog. What is more remarkable is where they are found. Roughly two-thirds of them are located in the arms rather than the head, so that each arm can taste, touch and make decisions to a considerable extent on its own. Even more puzzling is the animal's short life. Most species live only a year or two, and the young never meet their parents. High intelligence is normally found in long-lived creatures that have time to learn from their relatives, so the octopus seems to break the rules.

C  Laboratory experiments confirm what the keepers suspected. In a series of studies, Dr Helen Okoro of Dunmore University gave octopuses a transparent jar with a crab inside and the lid screwed on. Most of the animals worked out how to open it, usually after several attempts. Once they had succeeded, they opened later jars in a fraction of the time. Crucially, octopuses that had watched a neighbour open a jar were no quicker than those that had not, which suggests that they improve through their own experience rather than by imitation. Behaviour in the wild is just as striking. One species has been filmed collecting discarded coconut shells and carrying them across the seabed in an awkward shuffle that slows the animal down and exposes it to predators. Later, the octopus assembles the shells into a shelter. The animal is, in effect, accepting a cost now for a benefit later, something once thought to be the preserve of humans and a few other mammals.

D  Octopuses also seem to have personalities. Some are bold and explore every new object, while others hide in the corner of the tank for weeks. Keepers become convinced that individual animals recognise them, and one experiment has put that belief to the test. At a marine laboratory, two members of staff wore identical uniforms. One always fed the octopuses, while the other always prodded them gently with a bristle brush. Within a week, the animals were squirting jets of water at the person with the brush and ignoring the one who fed them, even when the two swapped places in the room. They had learned to tell the two humans apart, an ability that most invertebrates are not thought to possess.

E  Why should an animal so unlike us have evolved such a capable mind? The most popular theory points to the loss of the shell. Soft-bodied and without protection, early octopuses were vulnerable, and survival depended on outwitting predators rather than hiding from them. Their food, too, such as crabs in hard shells, rewarded cunning and dexterity. A body with eight flexible arms and no skeleton also poses extraordinary problems of control, and a large and complicated nervous system may have evolved to solve them. Notably, the leading explanation of intelligence in primates cannot apply here. According to that theory, large brains developed to cope with the demands of social life, but octopuses are solitary and spend almost their whole lives alone.

F  Not every scientist is convinced that the evidence is as strong as it looks. Measuring intelligence in an animal with such a different body is extremely difficult, and many tests assume that the subject is motivated by food and has a good sense of sight. Most have been designed around tasks that suit mammals, so they may even underestimate what an octopus can do. Other researchers point out that most experiments take place in captivity, where a bored animal in a small tank may behave more inventively than it ever would in the wild. A few scientists also warn against reading human thoughts into the behaviour of a creature whose last common ancestor with us lived more than 500 million years ago.

G  Whatever the final answer, the debate has already had practical consequences. Several countries have recently extended their animal-welfare laws to cover octopuses, and some now require that they be anaesthetised before being killed. Proposals to farm octopuses for food have met fierce opposition, partly because the animals would be kept in crowded tanks that offer very little to explore. If a solitary creature that lives for two years can solve problems, recognise individuals and plan ahead, we may have to rethink what we mean by intelligence, and what we owe to those who have it.

passages.title: Is free public transport worth the fare?
paras: A  Every few years, a city announces that its buses and trams will be free, and every few years the idea is hailed as a bold answer to congestion, pollution and inequality. The appeal is obvious. Removing fares seems to remove the main barrier between citizens and public transport, and it makes a simple, memorable slogan for a politician. Yet the economics are less straightforward than the slogans suggest, and the evidence from places that have tried the policy deserves more attention than it usually receives. In my view, much of the enthusiasm rests on a confusion between what is popular and what is effective. A policy can be loved by voters and still be a poor way of spending scarce public money, and the two questions should be kept apart.

B  Start with the money. In most cities, fares cover only part of the cost of running a network, commonly between a quarter and a half, with the rest coming from taxes. Abolishing fares therefore means finding a large sum of replacement income, and councils tend to assume that the amount is modest. It is not. Admittedly, some savings follow, since ticket machines, inspectors and cash handling disappear, and boarding is quicker, so vehicles spend less time at stops. But these savings seldom exceed a fifth of the lost revenue, and the gap must be filled either by higher taxes or by cuts elsewhere in the transport budget. Those cuts usually fall on maintenance and new vehicles, whose effects are slow to appear and easy for voters to overlook.

C  The next question is who actually uses the free service. Marden Bay, a medium-sized port city, introduced free buses in 2016, and the early results were celebrated. Passenger numbers rose by almost a third within two years. A survey of the new passengers, however, told a more sober story. Only a small fraction had previously driven; most had walked or cycled, or were making journeys that they would not otherwise have made at all. Car traffic fell by only two per cent. One city proves nothing, but the pattern has been reported elsewhere, and, since the hope was that free fares would empty the roads, I find the result disappointing for anyone who shared that hope. People who give up a healthy walk for a bus ride have not helped the environment.

D  Supporters respond that the rise in passengers is real and that the social benefits are worth paying for. They have a point. In poorer households, transport can account for a large share of income, and a free bus pass may make it possible to reach a better job or a hospital appointment. But this argument supports help for those who need it, rather than a universal subsidy. A well-paid commuter who rides the tram to the office receives exactly the same benefit as a student who cannot afford the fare, and the council pays for both. Targeted concessions would deliver most of the fairness at a fraction of the cost.

E  There is a further danger. When fares vanish and the budget stays the same, there is little money to improve the service. Marden Bay was forced to reduce the frequency of buses on quieter routes in the third year in order to balance its books, and the crowding on busy routes grew worse. This matters because surveys consistently show that passengers value frequency and reliability above price. Motorists are persuaded to leave their cars at home when the bus is faster and more dependable, not when it is cheaper. For someone who already spends heavily on fuel, insurance and parking, even a generous fare saving is small, and I doubt that it would tempt many of them.

F  There are cheaper ways of attracting passengers. Simplified fares, daily price caps and free travel for children and older people all help. So do investments that make buses quicker. The city of Calder spent a modest sum on dedicated bus lanes and traffic-light priority, and journey times fell by around a fifth. Ridership rose by almost as much as it did in Marden Bay, at a much lower cost to the taxpayer, and the money from fares went on paying for the improvements. Bus drivers also reported fewer delays, which in turn made the timetable easier to keep. In my judgement, a policy that makes the service better is likely to give a stronger return than one that merely makes it free.

G  None of this means that free public transport is always a mistake. In small towns, where fares bring in little money and congestion is not a problem, abolishing them may make sense, and a temporary free period can help to win back passengers after a crisis. But as a general model for large cities, the evidence is thin. Policymakers should be honest that free transport is a social policy rather than a traffic policy, and judge it by that standard.
